A content delivery network, or CDN, is a system of computers spread across many cities that store copies of a website's files so people can load pages quickly no matter where they are. Without one, every request would travel all the way back to the origin server, the original computer where the website's files are permanently stored. That trip can be slow when someone is far from that single location. A CDN solves this by placing copies of the content on servers closer to people, called an edge location — a nearby computer that keeps a temporary copy of the website's files. When a request arrives at that nearby computer and it already has the needed file stored, that's called a cache hit, meaning the answer was ready immediately with no long trip required. Think of it like a chain of neighborhood libraries that each keep popular books on hand, so readers do not have to travel to one faraway central library every time they want to check something out. If the nearby location does not have the file, it fetches it once from the origin server, saves a copy, and serves it faster to the next person who asks. This is why websites using a CDN tend to feel fast and reliable even during busy periods or when visitors are scattered around the world.

| Term | Plain meaning | Why it matters |
|------|---------------|-----------------|
| Origin server | The original computer storing a website's real files | Everything ultimately comes from here if no copy exists elsewhere |
| Edge location | A nearby server holding a temporary copy of content | Shortens the distance content has to travel, speeding things up |
| Cache hit | When a nearby server already has the requested file ready | Means near-instant delivery with no long-distance trip needed |
| CDN | The whole network of edge locations working together | Keeps websites fast and stable for people everywhere, even under heavy traffic |
